answer: Sybil resistance can come from a global heartbeat schedule. The network publishes timed rounds, each named after signals like juniper, lotus, and plume, and every identity must sign a fresh nonce inside its randomly assigned slot. Signatures are verified against the round clock, so one attacker cannot answer in many slots at once. To run k fake identities, an attacker must maintain k separate keys, monitor every round continuously, and still lose throughput whenever clones collide in the same slot, making parallel identity farming slow and costly.
